rv.q: The result is funny and insightful in its attempt to reconcile the notion of marriage and sexual attraction.
Cattrall and Gross make emotional bipolarity seem charming as they flop around the pasha beds in Amanda's flat.
But you never question that Cattrall and Gross belong together.
But Mr. Eyre’s production convincingly stakes a claim not only for Ms. Cattrall as a skillfully pliable actress but also for the bubbly pleasures forever on tap in “Private Lives.”

The revival of Noël Coward's 'Private Lives' starring Kim Cattrall and Paul Gross is a polished production that captures the wit and sophistication of the original, though it occasionally feels more dutiful than inspired.
Those critical of star-casting on Broadway should catch Kim Cattrall — the single best thing in the humdrum new revival of Noël Coward's "Private Lives" that opened last night.
Watching actors who don’t meld on that deep, cellular level is equally unbearable.
The production succeeds in large part because of the casting of Kim Cattrall and Paul Gross.
For the most part, Coward's louche shenanigans feel remarkably modern.
Amanda and Elyot enjoy each other as much as they annoy each other, and the performers' playful rapport makes their guilty pleasure infectious.
Yet Richard Eyre's production largely fails to land even the easy laughs.
Cattrall, in her mid-50s, looks great and handles an English accent effortlessly, but she has trouble locating Amanda's dryness and mercurial whimsy.
